segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now the apostles and the brothers and sisters throughout Judea heard that the Gentiles too had received the word of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when Peter went up to Jerusalem, the circumcised believers took issue with him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You went into the house of uncircumcised men and ate with them.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Peter began and laid it out for them in order, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I was in the city of Joppa praying, and in a trance I saw a vision: an object like a large sheet coming down, lowered from heaven by its four corners, and it came right up to me.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: I stared at it and looked closely, and I saw the four-footed animals of the earth, the wild beasts, the crawling creatures, and the birds of the sky.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: I also heard a voice saying to me, ‘Get up, Peter; slaughter and eat.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: But I said, ‘By no means, Lord, for nothing common or unclean has ever entered my mouth.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: But a voice from heaven answered a second time, ‘What God has made clean, you must not call common.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: This happened three times, and then everything was pulled up again into heaven.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And at that very moment three men arrived at the house where we were, sent to me from Caesarea.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: The Spirit told me to go with them, making no distinction. These six brothers also came with me, and we entered the man’s house.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: He told us how he had seen the angel standing in his house and saying, ‘Send to Joppa and summon Simon, who is called Peter;

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: he will speak words to you by which you will be saved, you and all your household.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell on them, just as on us at the beginning.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And I remembered the word of the Lord, how he used to say, ‘John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So if God gave them the same gift he gave us when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I to be able to stand in God’s way?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they heard this, they fell silent, and they glorified God, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “So then, even to the Gentiles God has given the turning back that leads to life.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now those who had been scattered by the trouble that arose over Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch, speaking the word to no one except Jews.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But some of them were men from Cyprus and Cyrene, who came to Antioch and began speaking to the Greek speakers as well, announcing the good news about the Lord Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number who believed turned to the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The report about them reached the ears of the assembly in Jerusalem, and they sent Barnabas out as far as Antioch.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he arrived and saw the grace of God, he rejoiced, and he urged them all to stay with the Lord with resolute hearts,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith. And a large crowd was added to the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he went off to Tarsus to look for Saul,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and when he found him, he brought him to Antioch. So it was that for a whole year they met with the assembly and taught a large crowd, and that in Antioch the disciples were first called Christians.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In those days prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: One of them, named Agabus, stood up and indicated through the Spirit that a great famine was about to come over the whole inhabited world; this took place under Claudius.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The disciples decided that each of them, according to their means, would send aid to the brothers and sisters living in Judea.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This they did, sending it to the elders by the hand of Barnabas and Saul.

notes.traditional: they that were of the circumcision; the circumcision party
notes.note: The Greek is literally ‘those from circumcision’. It may mean simply the Jewish believers, who at this point made up nearly the whole Jerusalem community, or a stricter group among them who insisted on circumcision. The text does not settle which, and translations divide.

The Greek is blunter: literally ‘men having a foreskin’. The complaint is not that Peter preached to Gentiles but that he accepted their hospitality and ate at their table, which observant Jews generally avoided because of the food laws. The sentence can also be read as a question (‘Why did you go in…?’), as some translations have it.

In Jewish usage ‘common’ was the opposite of ‘holy’: ordinary, not set apart, and so off limits to someone keeping the food laws. Some translations use ‘profane’ or ‘impure’. Verse 9 uses the related verb, literally ‘do not make common’, meaning to treat or declare something as defiled.

The verb can mean either to hesitate or to draw a distinction. The form used here favours ‘making no distinction’ (between Jew and Gentile), but many translations render ‘without hesitation’, as in the parallel account at 10:20, where the form is different. The same verb lies behind ‘took issue’ in verse 2.

‘Repentance’ now suggests mainly feeling sorry. The Greek word, shaped by the prophets’ call to return to God, means a change of direction in mind and conduct. Most translations keep ‘repentance’ as an established term understood to include a changed life.

The Greek word is a general one for pressure, distress or affliction, not the specific word for persecution, which Acts uses at 8:1 for the same events. Most translations render ‘persecution’ here because that is what the trouble was.

Manuscripts are divided between ‘Hellenists’ (Greek speakers) and ‘Greeks’. The SBLGNT prints the former, and it is translated here. At 6:1 the same word refers to Greek-speaking Jews, but the contrast with ‘no one except Jews’ in verse 19 shows that non-Jews are meant here, which is why many translations simply say ‘Greeks’.

notes.phrase: announcing the good news about the Lord Jesus
notes.note: The verb was an ordinary word for publicly announcing good news, with Jesus as its direct object here. ‘Preach’ and ‘gospel’ have since become church terms; many modern translations render much as this one does.

A first-century hearer knew this word as a civic gathering and as the Greek Old Testament’s term for Israel assembled. ‘Church’ now suggests a building or an institution. ‘Church’ is the near-universal rendering, and readers know what it refers to; ‘assembly’ is used here to keep the original associations.

The name has a Latin-style ending meaning ‘adherents of Christ’, like ‘Herodians’ for supporters of Herod. Most scholars think outsiders coined it, since believers in Acts call themselves disciples or brothers and sisters. The word occurs only three times in the New Testament (here, Acts 26:28 and 1 Peter 4:16).

The Greek word means the inhabited world, and in everyday use often amounted to the Roman Empire. Claudius was emperor from 41 to 54 CE. Ancient writers report food shortages in several regions during his reign, and Josephus records a severe famine in Judea in the mid-40s; no single empire-wide famine is attested.

candidates.reason: The plural shifts between ‘nations’ and ‘Gentiles’ across the New Testament, and a consistent rule for when each applies is needed.
Translations vary among tribulation, affliction, distress, persecution and trouble, and the word recurs across the Gospels, letters and Revelation.
Occurs at Acts 6:1, 9:29 and 11:20 with different referents, so one rendering (‘Hellenists’ or ‘Greek speakers’) should be fixed for all three.
Rendered variously as world, inhabited world, or empire in Luke-Acts, Hebrews and Revelation, and needs to be kept distinct from κόσμος.
The ritual sense (common, profane, defiled, impure) and its verb κοινόω recur in Mark 7, Acts 10–11, Romans 14 and Hebrews and should match across those passages.

warnings: Verse 20: εὐαγγελίζω is not rendered with a register form (announce the good news) and has no register-exception note.
